earlier_scan.source_named: Tallman, Adam J. R. (2018) A grammar of Chacobo, a southern Pano language (PhD, UT Austin; covers Pacahuara as near-identical variety) - repository returned 403

new_statements.quote: The surface pitch patterns of Pacahuara lexical items elicited in isolation tend to be distinct from Chácobo in all cases. Nearly all of phonological differences stated above make reference to the supposed prosodic categories (prominent syllable, tone, stress) of Pacahuara. But the prosodic system of Pacahuara is not understood and so the statements are at best tentative starting points for analysis. [...] Pacahuara should be studied in its own right not as derivative or dialectal variant of Chácobo. [p.35:] In Pacahuara a glottal stop occurs in the coda position of the first syllable of a lexical item as in (1.1). It is unclear whether this is related to metrical structure or prominence. In Pacahuara the glottal stop does not occur when the first syllable has the highest pitch (or high tone?)

new_statements.rule_in_words: No placement rule: the sole first-hand source states that Pacahuara's prosodic system (stress/tone/prominence) is not yet understood; isolated words show pitch patterns different from Chácobo, and a first-syllable coda glottal stop alternates with first-syllable highest pitch, possibly prominence-related.
new_statements.exceptions: None; author flags possible Chácobo interference in all Pacahuara data (speakers bilingual, heavy contact).
new_statements.domain_note: Observations are on lexical items elicited in isolation (citation forms) with surface pitch transcribed; no word- vs phrase-level analysis.
new_statements.identity_note: Tallman 2018 §1.11 describes the speech of the single remaining Tapanahua (Pacahuara) family living among the Chácobo at Puerto Tujuré (3 speakers in 2018), which he treats as a language distinct from Chácobo (chac1251); Fleck 2013 and SAPhon treat Pakawara as a dialect of Chácobo. The Chácobo stress rule (stem-initial by default, second syllable if H-toned;../chac1251/) is NOT asserted for Pacahuara by Tallman, who says Pacahuara surface pitch patterns differ from Chácobo 'in all cases'. East & East's 1969-70 SIL 'Pacaguara' microfiches document an earlier generation of (presumably) the same group.

sources.note: First-hand notes on the last speakers: Pacahuara surface pitch patterns on isolated words differ from Chácobo; a first-syllable coda glottal stop is absent 'when the first syllable has the highest pitch (or high tone?)'; 'It is unclear whether this is related to metrical structure or prominence'; p.38: 'the prosodic system of Pacahuara is not understood and so the statements are at best tentative starting points for analysis.' No stress-placement rule given.
